raw_case_text:
A five year old boy, diagnosed at the age of four with an ALL without central nervous system involvement or unfavourable cytogenetic features, presented with a history of fever, neutropenia and a painful right leg since four days and a right lower lobe consolidation with unilateral pleural effusion on chest X-ray. At that time he was treated for one year according to Dutch Childhood Oncology Group (DCOG) ALL-10 intermediate risk protocol. Due to persisting fever after 4 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftazidime and teicoplanin), the negative blood cultures and the abnormal findings on chest radiography, the patient was admitted to our hospital.
Physical examination at this time revealed no abnormal cardiac sounds, no abnormal breathing sounds, no hepatic or splenic enlargement, no lymphadenopathy and no signs of inflammation of the right leg. Laboratory studies showed a haemoglobin value of 6.3 mmol/l (after blood transfusion) and a leuco- and thrombocytopenia (leucocytes 0.6 x 109/l; thrombocytes 50 x 109/l). Blood chemistry showed an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP 145 mg/l). 
Additional diagnostic studies to detect a causative agent were done. Blood cultures taken were repeatedly negative for bacteria and fungi. Urine culture and faeces were negative for fungal pathogens. The multiple sputum cultures taken did not reveal any microorganisms. Cultures of both pleural fluid obtained by transthoracic puncture and broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) were negative for viral, bacterial and fungal agents. Aspergillus-antigen (galactomannan) was not detected in multiple plasma samples, pleural fluid and BAL fluid. Bone marrow aspirate to rule out a relapse of his leukaemia showed no malignant cells and cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria were negative. Urine tested negative for Legionella antigen. Ciprofloxacin was added to the antimicrobial therapy, to cover atypical causative agents of pneumonia. Empiric anti-fungal therapy was not initiated because of the stable condition of the patient and the negative test results at that moment.
Despite broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment (ceftazidime, teicoplanin and addition of ciprofloxacin for two days), fever persisted although the clinical condition remained stable. After 7 days, the developed a hepatomegaly and blood tests results showed still a pancytopenia, an elevated CRP (192 mg/l) and increased liver enzymes. Ultrasound examination of the abdomen confirmed the hepatomegaly without any focal lesions which might have been suggestive for fungal infection. 
 On day 10 he was transferred to the paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) of our hospital because of progressive respiratory distress and signs of a capillary leakage syndrome. At this time, the urine and faeces cultures became positive for Candida glabrata, while one out of many sputum samples grew Aspergillus fumigatus. Physical examination at this time showed a pale, moaning boy in respiratory distress needing supplementary oxygen via a non-rebreathing mask. On the nail of digit III of the left foot and on the soles of both feet small vasculitis-like lesions were noticed. Because of imminent respiratory failure the patient was intubated and artificial ventilated. Chest X-ray showed the known consolidation in the right lower lobe, but also pulmonary oedema with haziness of the perihilar regions. Transoesophageal ultrasound examination of the heart showed hypocontractility, with a round left intra-atrial tumour mass, compromising almost the whole left atrium (Figure 1). Suspicion of a fungal mass or infected thrombus together with the recovery of fungal pathogens in urine, faeces and sputum, led to the initiation of antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B. Progressive hemodynamic failure developed without an effect of high-dose inotropic medication and the clinical condition of the patient deteriorated fast. Several hours after admission to the PICU the patient died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented with a 4-day history of persistent fever, neutropenia, and right leg pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with standard/intermediate-risk ALL at age 4 and treated for 1 year per the DCOG ALL-10 protocol, the boy developed fever, neutropenia, right leg pain, and a right lower lobe consolidation with unilateral pleural effusion on chest X-ray. Because fever persisted after 4 days of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (ceftazidime and teicoplanin) with negative blood cultures, he was transferred to our hospital, where fever continued and he developed hepatomegaly on day 7 followed by acute respiratory failure, capillary leak syndrome, and refractory shock on day 10.
subjective.past_medical_history: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) without CNS involvement or unfavorable cytogenetics, diagnosed at age 4 and treated for 1 year on the Dutch Childhood Oncology Group (DCOG) ALL-10 intermediate-risk protocol.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent fever, right leg pain, and subsequent acute respiratory distress.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission exam showed normal heart and lung sounds, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, and no local signs of inflammation in the right leg. On day 7, clinical hepatomegaly developed. On day 10 (PICU transfer), he was pale, moaning, and in severe respiratory distress with capillary leak syndrome and small vasculitis-like lesions on the nail of the left third toe and the soles of both feet.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed post-transfusion hemoglobin 6.3 mmol/L, severe leukopenia (WBC 0.6 x 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 50 x 10^9/L), and elevated CRP (145 mg/L, rising to 192 mg/L with elevated liver enzymes on day 7). Repeated blood cultures, urine Legionella antigen, and bone marrow aspirate (ruling out leukemia relapse and bacterial/mycobacterial infection) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound on day 7 confirmed hepatomegaly without focal lesions. Chest X-ray on day 10 showed persistent right lower lobe consolidation with new perihilar pulmonary edema. On day 10, urine and stool cultures grew Candida glabrata and one sputum sample grew Aspergillus fumigatus.
objective.advanced_workup: Pleural fluid (via thoracentesis) and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cultures were negative for viral, bacterial, and fungal pathogens, and serial galactomannan antigen assays in plasma, pleural fluid, and BAL fluid were all negative. On day 10 in the PICU, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed myocardial hypocontractility and a large round left intra-atrial mass occupying nearly the entire left atrium.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal invasive fungal infection with a large left intra-atrial fungal mass/infected thrombus, right lower lobe pneumonia, cutaneous septic/vasculitic emboli, and refractory septic/cardiogenic shock in a neutropenic child with ALL, supported by isolation of Aspergillus fumigatus in sputum and Candida glabrata in urine and stool on day 10 despite negative plasma/pleural/BAL galactomannan and blood cultures. Treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftazidime, teicoplanin, ciprofloxacin), mechanical ventilation, high-dose inotropes, and initiation of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B upon detection of the atrial mass on day 10; the patient died of progressive hemodynamic failure several hours after PICU admission.
